title: Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models are surprisingly brittle to the ordering of premises in reasoning tasks, despite the fact that such ordering does not alter the underlying task. This paper investigates the effect of premise order on large language models and finds that they achieve the best performance when the premise order follows the intermediate reasoning steps to solve the problem.

sections.title: The Core Insight
sections.content:
Imagine you're trying to solve a logic puzzle. You have a set of rules and facts, but the order in which you're presented with them matters. For humans, the order of premises can make a problem easier or harder to solve. But what about large language models?

It turns out that the order of premises has a significant impact on their performance, even when the underlying task remains the same.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
The researchers created a benchmark to test the effect of premise order on large language models. They found that the models perform best when the premise order follows the ground truth proof.

But what happens when the premise order is changed? The models' performance drops significantly, with some models experiencing a drop of over 30%.

config.title: Performance Drop with Premise Order Change

sections.title: Benchmark Results
sections.content:
The researchers evaluated the performance of several large language models on the benchmark, including GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo, PaLM 2-L, and Gemini 1.0 Pro.

The results show that all models experience a significant drop in performance when the premise order is changed, with GPT-4-turbo experiencing a drop of 20-30% and Gemini 1.0 Pro experiencing a drop of over 40%.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
The premise order effect has significant implications for the development of large language models. It highlights the need for models to be able to reason effectively regardless of the order of premises.

This is particularly important for applications where the order of premises may not be controlled, such as in natural language processing tasks.

sections.title: Key Innovations
sections.content:
The researchers introduced a new benchmark, R-GSM, to evaluate the premise order effect on mathematical reasoning tasks.

The benchmark consists of 220 pairs of problems, including both the original problem and a manually rewritten version with a different premise order.

sections.title: Try It Yourself
sections.content:
You can try out the R-GSM benchmark and experiment with different premise orders to see how it affects the performance of large language models.

This can help you better understand the premise order effect and its implications for natural language processing tasks.
